title: Putting a business idea into practice

steps.title: Aims and objectives: what the business is for
steps.body:
An **aim** is what the business wants to achieve overall; an **objective** is a measurable target on the way to it. *Be the best-known bakery in town* is an aim; *sell 500 loaves a week by December* is an objective.

The specification splits objectives into two kinds.

**Financial**: survival, profit, sales, market share, financial security.

**Non-financial**: social objectives, personal satisfaction, challenge, independence and control.

Why they differ between businesses: a start-up's first objective is usually **survival**, because most new businesses fail in their first years. An established business aims for profit or market share. A social enterprise puts a community objective first. And many small businesses exist because the owner wanted to be their own boss, so independence matters more to them than growth.

rows: sell 500 a week; 10% of local market
enough saved to survive a bad month
employ people the job market overlooks
props.title: Business objectives on the specification

visuals.alt: A table of financial and non-financial objectives with an example of each

check.prompt: Which objective is most likely to come first for a business in its first year?
check.solution: Most new businesses fail early, so simply staying in business is the first hurdle. Market share and financial security come later.

steps.title: Revenue, costs and profit
steps.body:
Three quantities, three formulas, and they are the ones the exam uses:

$$\text{Revenue} = \text{price} \times \text{quantity sold}$$

$$\text{Total costs} = \text{fixed costs} + \text{variable costs}$$

$$\text{Profit} = \text{revenue} - \text{total costs}$$

**Fixed costs** do not change with output: rent, salaries, insurance, loan repayments. **Variable costs** rise with every unit made: materials, packaging, the electricity that runs the machines.

If profit comes out negative, the business has made a **loss**.

The word to be careful with is *revenue*. It is the money that comes in from sales, before any costs are taken off. Students lose marks by calling it profit.

visuals.alt: A card with the three formulas: revenue is price times quantity, total costs are fixed plus variable, profit is revenue minus total costs

check.prompt: A shop sells 150 T-shirts at £12 each. Calculate its revenue.

steps.title: A month in a small bakery
steps.body: Every profit question is the same three lines in the same order: revenue, total costs, then the difference. Write each line, with its label, and the method marks are safe even if the arithmetic slips.

visuals.problem: Priya's bakery: 800 loaves at £2.50; rent and wages £1200; ingredients £0.90 a loaf

steps.note: A profit, but a small one: £80 on £2000 of sales

check.prompt: Using Priya's figures, what would her profit be if she sold 900 loaves instead of 800?
check.solution: Revenue $= 2.50 \times 900 = 2250$. Variable $= 0.90 \times 900 = 810$. Total costs $= 1200 + 810 = 2010$. Profit $= 2250 - 2010 = £240$. Every extra loaf adds £1.60.

steps.title: Break-even: the sales that cover the costs
steps.body:
The **break-even level of output** is the number of units a business must sell for revenue to equal total costs: no profit, no loss.

$$\text{Break-even output} = \dfrac{\text{fixed costs}}{\text{price} - \text{variable cost per unit}}$$

The bottom of the fraction, price minus variable cost, is what each sale **contributes** towards the fixed costs. Sell at £25 with a variable cost of £10, and every sale puts £15 towards the rent. With £6000 of fixed costs, that takes $6000 \div 15 = 400$ sales.

On the chart, revenue is a straight line from the origin and total costs is a straight line that starts at the fixed costs. Where they cross is break-even. Left of it, costs are above revenue: a loss. Right of it, revenue is above costs: profit.

visuals.alt: A break-even chart: a revenue line from the origin, a total costs line starting at 6000, a dashed fixed costs line at 6000, and the crossing point marked at 400 units

check.prompt: Fixed costs are £3000, the price is £20 and the variable cost per unit is £8. Calculate the break-even output.

steps.title: Reading the chart: margin of safety and what moves the lines
steps.body:
**Margin of safety** is how far actual sales are above break-even:

$$\text{Margin of safety} = \text{actual output} - \text{break-even output}$$

It is the fall in sales the business could survive before making a loss. A margin of 250 units on 650 sales is comfortable; a margin of 10 is living on the edge.

The chart also shows what changes do. A **price rise** steepens the revenue line, so it crosses the cost line sooner: break-even falls. A **rise in variable costs** steepens the total cost line: break-even rises. A **rise in fixed costs** lifts the whole cost line: break-even rises. The exam asks these as *what happens to break-even if...*, and the answer is always in the formula.

visuals.alt: The same break-even chart with actual output of 650 units marked to the right of the 400-unit break-even point, showing the margin of safety

steps.text: Or: 250 units above break-even, each contributing £15: $250 \times 15 = £3750$
steps.note: Same answer both ways, which is a good check

check.prompt: Break-even is 400 units. Fixed costs rise from £6000 to £7500 with price £25 and variable cost £10 unchanged. Calculate the new break-even output.
check.solution: $7500 \div (25 - 10) = 7500 \div 15 = 500$ units. Higher fixed costs need more sales to cover them.

steps.title: Cash is not profit
steps.body:
**Cash** is the money actually in the bank. A business needs it every day: to pay suppliers, wages, rent and bills when they fall due. Run out of cash and the business cannot pay, and a business that cannot pay its debts is **insolvent** and can be closed, however profitable it looks on paper.

That last phrase is the point. **Profit** is revenue minus costs over a period. **Cash flow** is money in and money out, with its timing. They differ because:

- Customers may pay weeks after the sale, but suppliers want paying now.
- Buying a van or a machine takes all the cash at once, but the profit figure spreads the cost over years.
- Stock bought and not yet sold has used cash but earned nothing yet.

More new businesses fail from running out of cash than from making a loss.

visuals.problem: Profitable and broke in the same month

steps.text: Leo takes a £6000 furniture order in March: £2000 of timber, £1500 of labour, £2500 profit when delivered
He pays for the timber in March. The customer pays on delivery in May
March: cash out £3500, cash in £0. The bank balance falls, and the timber supplier's bill is due
The order is profitable. The business is still short of cash in March

check.prompt: Which of these is the best reason a profitable business might be unable to pay a bill on time?
check.solution: Profit is about totals; cash is about timing. If money comes in after it has to go out, the business can be profitable and still have nothing in the account on the day a bill is due.
options: Customers pay later than the business has to pay its suppliers
Its revenue is lower than its costs

steps.title: The cash-flow forecast
steps.body:
A **cash-flow forecast** predicts the money in and out each month, so a shortage can be seen coming and an overdraft arranged before the bill arrives. Four lines matter:

$$\text{Net cash flow} = \text{total inflows} - \text{total outflows}$$

$$\text{Closing balance} = \text{opening balance} + \text{net cash flow}$$

The **closing balance** of one month is the **opening balance** of the next. That link is where the marks are lost: work down each column, then carry the closing figure across.

visuals.alt: A three-month cash-flow forecast with inflows, outflows, net cash flow, opening balance and closing balance, showing the closing balance carried forward as the next month's opening balance

steps.text: A negative closing balance in February: the business needs an overdraft of at least £700 that month
March opens at $-700$; net $= 1800$; closing $= £1100$. The shortage was temporary, which the forecast showed in advance
steps.note: The forecast's job is to reveal February before it happens

check.prompt: A business has an opening balance of £3000, inflows of £5000 and outflows of £6500 in a month. Calculate the closing balance.

steps.title: Where the money comes from
steps.body:
**Short-term** finance covers a cash shortage for weeks or months:

- **Overdraft**: the bank lets the account go below zero, up to a limit. Flexible, but interest is charged daily and the rate is high.
- **Trade credit**: a supplier lets the business pay 30 or 60 days after delivery. Free, if paid on time.

**Long-term** finance pays for starting up or growing:

- **Personal savings**: no interest and no loss of control, but limited, and the owner's own money is at risk.
- **Loans**: a fixed sum repaid with interest over years. Keeps ownership, but repayments are due whatever happens.
- **Retained profit**: profit kept in the business rather than paid out. Free, but only exists once the business is profitable.
- **Share capital**: selling shares in a company. No repayment, but the new shareholders own part of the business and its profit.
- **Venture capital**: investors who put money into risky start-ups for a share, often with advice attached.
- **Crowdfunding**: many small amounts from the public online, often in return for the product or a reward.

The choice always turns on the same question: does the owner want to **owe** money or **share** the business?

visuals.alt: A table of the sources of finance, whether each is short or long term, and the main cost of each

check.prompt: A start-up wants finance without giving away any ownership and without monthly repayments. Which source fits best?
check.solution: Savings involve no repayments and no new owners. Venture capital and share capital give away ownership; a loan means repayments.

steps.title: Your turn: work a break-even through
steps.body: Fixed costs £4000, price £20, variable cost £12 a unit. Work the break-even output one line at a time: contribution first, then the division.

visuals.fallback: Contribution per unit is $20 - 12 = £8$. Break-even $= 4000 \div 8 = 500$ units.

check.prompt: Same business: fixed costs £4000, price £20, variable cost £12. It sells 620 units. Calculate the margin of safety.
check.solution: Break-even is 500 units. Margin of safety $= 620 - 500 = 120$ units.

steps.title: Grade 9: the questions that combine two ideas
steps.body:
Section 1.3 is where Business asks you to calculate, and the top marks go to the questions that chain two calculations or read a change off a formula.

**Interest on a loan.** $\text{Interest (\%)} = \dfrac{\text{total repayment} - \text{amount borrowed}}{\text{amount borrowed}} \times 100$. Borrow £10 000, repay £11 500: interest is $1500 \div 10\,000 \times 100 = 15\%$.

**What happens to break-even if...** Do not guess; look at the formula. Anything that makes the bottom smaller, a lower price or a higher variable cost, raises break-even. A higher fixed cost raises it. A higher price lowers it, and the follow-up point is that fewer customers may buy.

**Profitable but out of cash.** The analyse question that catches people. The answer is timing: customers pay later than suppliers demand payment, and big purchases use cash at once. The cash-flow forecast exists to show that month in advance.

**Which source of finance.** It always turns on owe or share, and on whether the business already has the cash flow to meet repayments. A proven business can borrow; a risky start-up may have to give up equity.

steps.text: A business breaks even at 400 units and sells 650. Then rent rises by £1500
New margin of safety: $650 - 500 = 150$ units, down from 250
So the rent rise has cut the cushion by 100 units, and if sales drop 20% the business makes a loss
steps.note: The last line turns two numbers into a judgement

check.prompt: A business borrows £8000 and repays £9200 in total. Calculate the interest as a percentage of the amount borrowed.

steps.title: Summary
steps.body:
- **Objectives**: financial (survival, profit, sales, market share, security) and non-financial (social, satisfaction, challenge, independence). A start-up's first is survival.
- **Revenue** $=$ price $\times$ quantity. **Total costs** $=$ fixed $+$ variable. **Profit** $=$ revenue $-$ total costs.
- **Break-even output** $=$ fixed costs $\div$ (price $-$ variable cost per unit). Lower price or higher costs raise it.
- **Margin of safety** $=$ actual output $-$ break-even output.
- **Cash is not profit.** Timing of payments and one-off purchases mean a profitable business can run out of cash, and running out of cash is what closes businesses.
- **Net cash flow** $=$ inflows $-$ outflows. **Closing balance** $=$ opening $+$ net cash flow, and it becomes next month's opening balance.
- **Interest** $=$ (repayment $-$ borrowed) $\div$ borrowed $\times 100$.
- **Finance**: short-term is overdraft and trade credit; long-term is savings, loans, retained profit, shares, venture capital, crowdfunding. The choice is owe or share.

visuals.alt: A card with the five formulas: break-even output, margin of safety, net cash flow, closing balance and interest

questions.prompt: A stall sells 200 cups of coffee at £3 each. Calculate its revenue.
Which of these is a fixed cost for a café?
questions.solution: Rent is the same every month however many coffees are sold, so it is fixed. Beans, milk and cups rise with every sale, so they are variable.

questions.prompt: A business has fixed costs of £1200 a month and variable costs of £4 per unit. It makes 300 units. Calculate its total costs for the month.
Which of these is a non-financial objective?
questions.solution: Personal satisfaction, independence, challenge and social objectives are non-financial. Survival, profit, sales, market share and financial security are the financial ones.
options: Personal satisfaction from running the business

questions.prompt: A business has revenue of £8000, fixed costs of £2500 and variable costs of £3000. Calculate its profit.
questions.solution: Total costs $= 2500 + 3000 = £5500$. Profit $=$ revenue $-$ total costs $= 8000 - 5500 = £2500$.

questions.prompt: A business has fixed costs of £6000. It sells its product for £25 and the variable cost per unit is £10. Calculate the break-even level of output.
questions.solution: Break-even $=$ fixed costs $\div$ (price $-$ variable cost per unit) $= 6000 \div (25 - 10) = 6000 \div 15 = 400$ units. Each sale contributes £15 towards the £6000 of fixed costs.

questions.prompt: A business breaks even at 400 units and actually sells 650. Calculate its margin of safety.
questions.solution: Margin of safety $=$ actual output $-$ break-even output $= 650 - 400 = 250$ units. Sales could fall by 250 before it makes a loss.

questions.prompt: In one month a business has cash inflows of £9500 and cash outflows of £7200. Calculate its net cash flow.
A business starts the month with an opening balance of £1500. Its net cash flow for the month is $-£2000$. Calculate its closing balance.
questions.solution: Closing balance $=$ opening balance $+$ net cash flow $= 1500 + (-2000) = -£500$. A negative closing balance means the business needs an overdraft or it cannot pay its bills.

questions.prompt: Which of these is a short-term source of finance?
questions.solution: An overdraft and trade credit are short-term: they cover a cash shortage for weeks or months. Loans, share capital, venture capital, retained profit, personal savings and crowdfunding are long-term.
options: A bank loan repaid over five years

questions.prompt: A business has fixed costs of £6000, a variable cost of £10 per unit and sells at £25. It raises its price to £30. Calculate the new break-even level of output.
questions.solution: New contribution per unit $= 30 - 10 = £20$. Break-even $= 6000 \div 20 = 300$ units, down from 400. A higher price means each sale covers more fixed cost, so fewer sales are needed; the risk is that fewer customers buy at £30.

markScheme.description: compared with the old 400, or the effect stated

questions.prompt: A business borrows £10 000 and repays £11 500 in total over two years. Calculate the total interest as a percentage of the amount borrowed.
questions.solution: Interest $=$ total repayment $-$ amount borrowed $= 11\,500 - 10\,000 = £1500$. As a percentage of the loan: $1500 \div 10\,000 \times 100 = 15\%$.

questions.prompt: A business sells at £8 per unit with a variable cost of £3 per unit and fixed costs of £4000. It sells 1200 units. Calculate its profit.
questions.solution: Revenue $= 8 \times 1200 = £9600$. Total costs $= 4000 + 3 \times 1200 = 4000 + 3600 = £7600$. Profit $= 9600 - 7600 = £2000$. Check: break-even is $4000 \div 5 = 800$ units, and the 400 units above it each contribute £5, which is £2000.

questions.prompt: A business has an opening balance of £2000 in January. Net cash flow is $+£500$ in January and $-£3200$ in February. Calculate the closing balance at the end of February.
questions.solution: January closing $= 2000 + 500 = £2500$. February opening is the same £2500. February closing $= 2500 + (-3200) = -£700$. The closing balance of one month is the opening balance of the next; skipping that link is the usual error.

markScheme.description: carried forward as February's opening balance

questions.prompt: Leo's furniture business made a profit of £15 000 last year, but in March he could not pay his timber supplier on time. Analyse why a profitable business can still run short of cash.
questions.solution: Two chains rooted in Leo. Timing: he pays for timber when he buys it but customers pay for furniture weeks later on delivery, so in a month with a big order he has paid out before the cash has come in, and the profit exists on paper but not in the bank. Spending on assets: buying a new machine or a van uses cash now, while profit spreads the cost over years, so a profitable year can still empty the account. Level 3 links both to the supplier going unpaid.

markScheme.description: Level 1 (1 to 2): points made with limited development, little link to the case
Level 2 (3 to 4): one developed chain, applied to the business
Level 3 (5 to 6): two developed chains of reasoning, each applied to the business and reaching an outcome

criteria.text: Timing identified: Leo pays suppliers before customers pay him, applied to March
Developed to an outcome: cash leaves before it arrives, so the balance goes negative although the sale is profitable
A second cause: buying equipment or stock, or customers paying late, applied to a furniture maker
Developed to an outcome: a profitable year with an empty account, so the supplier goes unpaid

questions.modelAnswer: Profit and cash are measured differently. Profit is revenue minus costs for the year, but cash is what is actually in the bank on a given day. Leo pays for timber when he buys it, yet his customers pay for furniture when it is delivered, often weeks later. In March he may have bought timber for a large order that had not yet been paid for, so the money had gone out before it came in, and although the order will make a profit, the cash was not there to pay the supplier. A second reason is spending on things that are not day-to-day costs. If Leo bought a new machine or a van, the whole cost left his bank account at once, whereas in the profit figure that cost is spread over years, so a profitable business can still have an empty account. Both mean Leo needs a cash-flow forecast so he can see the shortfall coming and arrange an overdraft before the supplier's bill is due.

questions.prompt: Maya wants £50 000 to open a second branch of her successful café. A bank has offered a loan; an investor has offered the money in return for a 40% share of the business. Justify which source of finance Maya should choose.
questions.solution: Choose, argue both ways, name the deciding factor. Loan: Maya keeps full ownership and all future profit; interest is a known cost; but repayments are due every month whether or not the branch succeeds, and the bank may want security. Investor: no repayments and the investor may bring experience, but Maya gives up 40% of all future profit and some control for ever. Deciding factor: how confident Maya is in the second branch and whether she values control; a proven café with steady cash flow can service a loan.

markScheme.description: Level 1 (1 to 3): limited points, little application, no real judgement
Level 2 (4 to 6): developed reasoning for the choice with some application; a judgement is made
Level 3 (7 to 9): developed reasoning for the choice and against the alternative, applied throughout, with a justified judgement that names the deciding factor

criteria.text: A clear choice with developed reasons applied to Maya's café and the second branch
Developed reasons against the alternative, applied to the case
A judgement naming the deciding factor: ownership and control, the certainty of repayments, or the café's cash flow

questions.modelAnswer: Maya should take the bank loan. Her first café is already successful, so it produces the steady cash flow needed to meet monthly repayments, and once the loan is repaid she owns the second branch outright and keeps all of its profit. The interest is a known, fixed cost she can build into her plan. The investor's offer avoids repayments, which would matter if the new branch were slow to start, and an experienced investor might bring useful advice. But 40% of the business is a large price: Maya would give away 40% of the profit of both branches for as long as the business exists, far more than the interest on a £50 000 loan, and she would lose some control over decisions. The deciding factor is that Maya's business is proven. A start-up with no track record might need to give up equity because no bank would lend; a successful café can borrow, so the loan keeps her ownership and is cheaper in the long run.

questions.prompt: A business's variable cost per unit rises while its price and fixed costs stay the same. What happens to its break-even level of output?
questions.solution: Break-even $=$ fixed costs $\div$ (price $-$ variable cost). A higher variable cost shrinks the bottom of that fraction, so the answer is larger: more units must be sold before the fixed costs are covered.

markScheme.description: rises, because contribution per unit falls

options: It rises, because each sale contributes less towards the fixed costs
It falls, because costs are higher
It stays the same, because fixed costs have not changed

questions.prompt: Evaluate whether making a profit should be the most important objective for a business in its first year.
questions.solution: Both sides, applied, then it depends on. For profit: without it the business cannot pay its owner or reinvest, and lenders and investors expect it. Against: in the first year survival matters more, and survival is about cash, not profit; building a customer base may mean low prices and low profit at first; some owners' objectives are non-financial. Judgement: it depends on the type of business and how it is financed; a business with a loan to repay needs cash and survival first, while profit becomes the main objective once it is established.

markScheme.description: Level 1 (1 to 3): limited points, little application, no judgement
Level 2 (4 to 6): some developed reasoning with some application; a judgement without much support
Level 3 (7 to 9): developed chains on both sides, applied to the case, with a supported judgement
Level 4 (10 to 12): balanced, developed chains applied throughout, and a judgement that says what it depends on and how the answer would change

criteria.text: The case for profit as the main objective, developed: pays the owner, funds growth, satisfies lenders and investors
The case against, developed: survival and cash flow come first, building customers may cost early profit, non-financial objectives
Application to a first-year business throughout, with examples
A judgement that says what it depends on, the type of business and its finance, and how the answer changes once it is established

questions.modelAnswer: Profit matters to every business, because without it the owner cannot be paid, there is nothing to reinvest, and lenders or investors who expect a return will lose confidence. But in the first year profit is rarely the most important objective. A new business must first survive, and survival depends on cash rather than profit: a start-up can be profitable on paper and still fail because it cannot pay a supplier or the rent in a bad month, so managing cash flow comes first. Building a customer base often means low introductory prices, free samples or heavy promotion, all of which reduce profit now in order to earn more later. Many owners also start businesses for non-financial reasons, such as independence or doing something they believe in, and for them a small profit is enough. Whether profit should come first therefore depends on the type of business and how it is financed. A business that has borrowed heavily must generate cash to meet repayments and cannot afford a loss-making first year, so profit and cash both matter from the start. A business funded by savings, or one whose owner wants independence more than income, can treat survival and growth as the first-year objectives and make profit the priority once it is established.

examTechnique.body:
Section 1.3 is where Paper 1 puts its calculations, and they are worth learning to do fast: revenue, total costs, profit, break-even, margin of safety, net cash flow, closing balance and interest. Write the formula, substitute, answer with the unit. The formula line earns a mark even when the arithmetic slips, and it is the line most students leave out.

The traps are consistent. Revenue is not profit. Break-even goes up when the bottom of the fraction goes down. A closing balance becomes the next opening balance. And profit is not cash: the analyse question about a profitable business that cannot pay a bill is answered with the word timing.
examinerErrors: Calling revenue profit. Revenue is price times quantity, before any costs.
Forgetting to subtract the variable cost before dividing in the break-even formula, and dividing fixed costs by the price alone.
Saying break-even falls when variable costs rise. The contribution per unit falls, so more units are needed: break-even rises.
Not carrying the closing balance forward as the next month's opening balance in a cash-flow forecast.
Explaining a cash shortage as the business making a loss. A profitable business runs short of cash because of timing and one-off purchases.
Calculating interest as a percentage of the total repaid instead of the amount borrowed.
Recommending share capital or venture capital for a business that could borrow, without noticing it gives away part of the profit for ever.
examTechnique.grade9Looks: A grade 9 answer writes the formula before the numbers every time and gives the unit with the answer. It chains calculations when the question does, working out a new break-even and then a new margin of safety, and turns the numbers into a sentence about risk. It reads a change off the break-even formula rather than guessing. On cash it explains timing and one-off spending, and says what a cash-flow forecast is for. On finance it asks owe or share, checks whether the business has the cash flow to repay, and names that as the deciding factor.
